opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as a few core questions, and if you can't answer yes to most of them, RL probably isn't the right tool yet.

The first is: is there a clear, measurable objective? RL is ultimately an optimization machine, so you need a reward signal that actually captures what you care about. In data center cooling, for example, it was energy efficiency, something like PUE, subject to a set of safety constraints. If the operators themselves can't agree on what "good" looks like, or the objective is fuzzy and multi-stakeholder, the agent will happily optimize the wrong thing.

The second is: do you have enough data, and is it the right kind of data? Industrial systems usually have years of historical sensor logs, which is great, but that data reflects how humans have historically operated the system. It often covers a fairly narrow slice of the state-action space. So you have to ask whether there's enough natural variation to learn from, or whether you can safely explore, or whether you have a good enough simulator to fill the gaps.

Third is: do the controls actually matter? This sounds obvious, but a surprising number of systems are dominated by external factors like weather, demand, or upstream processes, and the actionable levers only move the outcome a little. You want a problem where better decisions translate into meaningful gains, and where the dynamics are complex enough, with lots of interacting variables and nonlinear effects, that a learned policy can beat hand-tuned heuristics or classic PID-style control.

Fourth, and in practice this is often the deciding factor, is safety and the cost of mistakes. Can you constrain the action space so the agent can never do something catastrophic? Can you keep a human in the loop or fall back to the existing control system? In the real world you don't get infinite resets the way you do in a game, so you need to architect the system so that even a bad recommendation is a recoverable one.

And finally, there's the operational question: can you actually close the loop? Is the infrastructure there to read sensors in near real time and write setpoints back to the control system, and are the operators willing to trust it? A lot of projects that look great on paper die because the plumbing or the organizational buy-in isn't there.

So my rough heuristic is: clear objective, sufficient data, meaningful controllable levers, complex dynamics, and a way to act safely. When those line up, RL can deliver results that are hard to get any other way. When they don't, you're often better off starting with simpler optimization or better instrumentation first.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL as optimizing a measurable reward subject to safety constraints, and says the problem needs sufficient historical data or a simulator to learn from. Together, these communicate constrained optimization grounded in data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's the question we spend the most time on before we ever write a line of code. The way I think about it is there's a checklist of maybe four or five things that need to be true.

The first one is: do you actually have a good simulator, or can you build one? Reinforcement learning is fundamentally about trial and error, and you cannot do trial and error on a real power plant or a real data center cooling system. You'll break things, or at minimum you'll make your operators very nervous. So the question becomes, can we build a model of the system that's faithful enough that a policy trained in simulation transfers to the real world? And that's where a lot of the hard work actually is. With data center cooling at Google, we had years of sensor data, so we could build predictive models of how temperature and power would respond to different setpoints. In industrial settings like what we work on at Phaidra, that's often the first phase of the project, just getting the data infrastructure to a point where you can trust the model.

The second thing is: is there actually a sequential decision-making problem here? A lot of times someone comes to you and says, "I want to use RL," and when you dig in, it's really a supervised learning problem or a static optimization. RL earns its keep when the decision you make now affects the state you'll be in later. Thermal systems are a great example because of the inertia. If I change a chiller setpoint, I don't see the full effect for twenty or thirty minutes, and the decision I make now constrains what I can do later. That's a real RL problem. If there's no temporal dependency, you probably shouldn't bother.

The third thing is: can I define the reward cleanly, and can I define the safety constraints cleanly? In industrial control, the reward is usually some combination of efficiency, throughput, and quality, and that's fine. But the constraints matter even more. There are usually hard operating limits that you can never violate, and you need a way to encode those such that the agent can't learn to cheat. One of the things we learned early is that if you leave a loophole, the agent will find it. It's very good at finding it.

And then the fourth thing, which people underestimate, is: how does the system fail, and can you fall back safely? Even with a great simulator, the real world will drift. Equipment degrades, sensors fail, seasons change. So you need a layer around the agent that monitors whether its actions make sense and can hand control back to the existing control system instantly. If you can't architect that safety layer, I'd argue you shouldn't deploy, no matter how good the policy looks offline.

There's one more thing I'd add, which is more cultural than technical. Is there an operator on the other side who's willing to work with you? Because the first version of the system is going to be recommendations, not autonomous control. And if the people who run the plant don't trust it, it doesn't matter how good it is. So part of my assessment is always, do we have a champion on the floor who wants this to work?

If all of those line up, then I get pretty excited, because the upside in these systems is enormous. If one or two are missing, we'll usually say, let's go fix those first, and then come back to the RL part.

r001.rationale: The response requires a data-grounded system model, a defined reward, and clearly specified safety constraints, which together communicate a constrained optimization formulation based on underlying data.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking whether it’s actually a sequential decision-making problem. Are you taking actions that change the state of a system, and do those changes affect the decisions you’ll need to make later? If you can make each decision independently, you may not need reinforcement learning.

Then there’s the practical question: can you learn how to control this system safely? Where does the experience come from? Do you have historical operating data, a simulator, or the ability to run carefully constrained experiments? In a real-world system, you usually can’t let an agent try arbitrary actions and learn from whatever breaks.

You also need a measurable objective, enough visibility into the system to make good decisions, and a clear definition of the constraints. What are you trying to improve, what can you actually control, and what must never happen?

And finally, I’d ask whether a simpler approach would work. The goal is to solve the control problem. Reinforcement learning becomes interesting when the consequences of your actions unfold over time and accounting for those consequences can meaningfully improve performance.

r001.rationale: The response mentions data sources, a measurable objective, and constraints, but it does not state that solvability depends on formulating the problem as a constrained optimization problem grounded in the underlying data.

sol-6.1.text:
I usually start by asking whether it’s a sequential decision-making problem. Are you making decisions that affect what happens next, and do those consequences influence the decisions you’ll make later? If so, reinforcement learning might be a useful framework.

Then there are the practical questions. Can you observe enough of the system to make good decisions? Can you define what good performance looks like? And can you learn safely, either from historical data, in a simulator, or through carefully constrained interaction with the real system?

That last part is especially important. In a real-world control problem, you can’t just let an agent explore freely and break things. You need constraints, a way to evaluate the policy, and a safe fallback. So I’d distinguish between whether you can formulate something as an RL problem and whether RL is actually the right tool to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sequential decision-making, safety constraints, and data or simulation for learning, but it does not state that solvability depends on formulating a constrained optimization problem grounded in the underlying data.
